ConocoPhillips fell 4.1% over two days (from $140.52 on Nov 16 to $134.48 today), despite oil prices holding relatively firm — US crude at $89.53 and global crude at $92.94. The sharp drop came as geopolitical tensions in the Middle East intensified, with Iran attacking U.S. installations in Kuwait and the IEA warning that the Strait of Hormuz — a critical global oil chokepoint — has lost credibility as a reliable energy corridor due to the Iran conflict. For an oil major like ConocoPhillips, this kind of regional instability typically pressures valuations even when current oil prices are stable, because it raises longer-term uncertainty about supply and operations.

The decline also reflects a broader energy market headwind: record diesel prices are now driving inflation higher in major economies like the UK, which could dampen fuel demand if central banks respond with tighter policy. Meanwhile, rising electricity demand from AI data centers is competing for investment capital and policy attention that might otherwise flow toward traditional energy infrastructure.
